author: ValWood
body:
* **PTHR ID & PTN node:**


GO:0061685 | diphthine methylesterase activity | IBA with S000000450 , PTN000522690

* **Sequences with problematic annotation (ID + gene/protein name):**

https://www.pombase.org/gene/SPCC18.15 and others

* **Type of Issue: Erroneous source or erroneous propagation, or other issue**

The primary annotation is fine, but its too early to propagate, becuse it probable that the catalytic activity doesnt reside in this subunit. Of 124 WD repeat proteins in PomBase, none have a catalytic activity provided by the WD rep[eat domains.

I checked into this because WD repeat domain-only proteins are not usually catalytic.
It seems dph7 is clearly part of this [athway but its MF is controversial, see this later review
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23971743/ 

Dph7 is required for the conversion from diphthine to diphthamide. Δdph7 yeast strain accumulates diphthine ([Su et al., 2012a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4280834/#R44)). Dph7 is a WD40 repeats containing protein and may mediate protein-protein interactions ([Su et al., 2012a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4280834/#R44)). However, the precise molecular function of Dph7 in diphthamide biosynthesis awaits further studies. As discussed above, methylated diphthamide is also found in Δdph7 ([Wei et al., 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4280834/#R53)). Dph5 was found to bind eEF2 more tightly in Δdph7 ([Carette et al., 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4280834/#R4), [Uthman et al., 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4280834/#R48)). Therefore, it has been proposed that Dph7 is responsible for either displacing Dph5 from EF2 or preventing the additional methylation. Dph7 has also been shown to participate in the retromer-mediated endosomal recycling pathway and named Ere1. ....Understanding the exact molecular function of Dph7 will help addressing this question. 

and
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28357244/
Consistent with roles in the amidation step, dph6 and dph7 deletion strains fail to complete diphthamide synthesis and accumulate diphthine-modified EF2. In contrast to Dph6, the catalytically relevant amidase, Dph7 appears to be regulatory.
